title: #126. Sticking Our Collective Heads in the Sand
author: Peter Gray
summary: Peter Gray argues that the widely accepted explanation for rising anxiety and depression among American schoolchildren since 2010, smartphones and social media, is not supported by the researchers most immersed in studying it, and that a more obvious culprit, the Common Core State Standards' overhaul of schooling itself, has been almost entirely ignored rather than actually refuted. He marshals evidence he considers hard to explain any other way: in every survey asking kids what stresses them, school always ranks first by a wide margin; anxiety, depression, and teen suicide rates measurably plummet every summer vacation and spike again every fall; and cross-national data correlates psychological distress with school-system stress characteristics, not smartphone availability. Gray is careful to specify Common Core's actual mechanism of harm, evaluating teachers and schools on narrow standardized test scores reduced teachers' freedom to engage students, increased time-wasting test drill, and cut into recess, changes that teachers and school psychologists themselves reported as increasing stress at the time. His closing argument is psychological rather than empirical: adults avoid blaming the school system because doing so would implicate themselves in allowing an abusive system to continue, and fixing it feels like a monumental task, making it far easier to blame "greedy social media companies" instead.
points: Gray's strongest single piece of evidence is the seasonal pattern: anxiety, depression, pediatric mental health admissions, and teen suicides measurably drop every summer vacation and rise again every fall when school resumes, a correlation that tracks the school calendar rather than smartphone adoption timelines.

He names Common Core's specific causal mechanism rather than blaming 'testing' vaguely: evaluating teachers, principals, and districts on narrow standardized-test scores reduced instructional freedom, increased time-wasting drill, and cut recess, changes teachers and school psychologists themselves reported as more stressful contemporaneously.

Gray explicitly bounds his claim to avoid overreach, acknowledging that abuse, addicted parents, or relentless bullying can dramatically outweigh school stress for individual children, while arguing school is still the dominant population-level factor because 'those sources of stress affect only a fraction of the total population of kids, while school affects essentially everyone.'

His explanation for why researchers and journalists have ignored rather than rebutted his hypothesis is explicitly psychological, not evidentiary: acknowledging school as the cause would implicate the adults who allow a compulsory system to continue, whereas blaming social media companies costs the public nothing to believe.
quotes: The data simply do not support the social media/smartphone hypothesis. But even those in authoritative positions who reject the media/smartphone hypothesis have so far almost uniformly avoided examining my alternative hypothesis, that a major change in how we do schooling, instituted by the Common Core State Standards, increased the stress of schooling and thereby elevated the rates anxiety and depression among school-aged kids, especially teens.
As I have said many times before, no adult would willingly accept a job that is anything like the schooling we impose on our kids. We would all see it as a job from hell.

Every year, when summer vacation from school begins, rates of anxiety, depression, pediatric mental health admissions, and teen suicides plummet, and every fall, when school starts again, those rates go up again. By some measures they double.

Common Core dictated that teachers, principals, and whole school districts would be evaluated based on the students' scores on standardized tests covering a narrow range of curriculum, especially math and literacy. The inevitable effect was reduction in teachers' freedom to adapt what they were doing to meet the needs and interests of students and truly engage students intellectually, and an increase in boring, time-wasting drill.

But those sources of stress affect only a fraction of the total population of kids, while school affects essentially everyone. That is why, in surveys of the whole population of kids, school always comes out on top as the major source of distress and those other causes are way down the list.

We simply don't want to believe that our public school system, which has long had an undeserved halo around it and where children are compelled by law to be, is a major source of children's suffering.
